heading: WHAT'S WORKING IN B2B GTM IN 2026 (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: A survey of 300 B2B software GTM leaders reveals five key trends for 2026: founder-led sales remains effective longer than expected, persisting through $10M ARR; traditional relationship-based channels like networking and intimate events outperform AI-driven alternatives on the GTM scorecard; AI search adoption surged to 39% core usage (up 11 points year-over-year), with companies now focused on measuring influence rather than just visibility; signal-based targeting remains immature with no consensus on which signals matter most, though content engagement (52%), website visits (42%), and product usage (40%) lead adoption; and Claude has become the dominant GTM tool, with Claude Code seeing particular popularity as GTM teams adopt more technical AI capabilities. The research warns that companies face a barbell dynamic where success comes from either exceptional relationships or exceptional AI execution, with messaging and positioning emerging as the next competitive frontier.
strategic_hook: Understanding which GTM channels and tools drive actual results for different company sizes and deal structures directly informs which customer acquisition strategies to prioritize in your business plan and competitive positioning against rivals using different customer engagement models.

heading: CITIZENLAB DETAILS NEW SPYWARE TRIGGERED BY ONLINE ADVERTISING (2 MINUTE READ)
summary: CitizenLab researchers discovered a new spyware called "AdFection" developed by Israeli firm Discover-Tech that infects devices through online advertising with zero user interaction required, marking the first confirmed case of government-backed zero-click spyware delivered via ads. The malware was deployed across 442 million ads on over 120,000 websites including the BBC and New York Times, targeting journalists at Al Jazeera and officials at NATO, the European Commission, NVIDIA, and Arm. Discover-Tech exploited real-time bidding auction systems used by ad platforms to profile and de-anonymize users before delivering malicious code embedded in innocent-looking ads. Google has since suspended Discover-Tech from its ad platform following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant. Senior researcher Bill Marczak warned that this discovery is likely "just the tip of the iceberg" and recommended users disable ad tracking or block ads entirely.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: HOW TO PITCH LOCAL NEWSROOMS IN THE US (9 MINUTE READ)
summary: Local newsrooms in the US have shrunk dramatically, with only 7.8 journalists per 100,000 residents in 2026 compared to 40 per 100,000 in 2002, creating an environment where overworked journalists are vastly outnumbered by PR professionals. Successful pitching to local outlets requires understanding their distinct structures: broadcast newsrooms revolve around assignment editors who set the daily agenda, while non-broadcast outlets operate through reporters and editors. The pitch strategy must match the outlet type and format—print needs ready-to-run stories with data, TV needs visuals and on-camera guests, and radio needs articulate speakers—and should include all information upfront to minimize back-and-forth with time-strapped journalists. Building an effective media list involves mapping core local outlets, sizing the newsroom by checking staff pages, and identifying journalists by researching their recent coverage using site-specific searches. Stories succeed locally when they have genuine community impact, feature local people or faces, provide strong visual elements for TV, and offer a timely hook that answers "why now?" The key to success is thinking like a producer: make journalists' jobs easier by targeting the right person, providing localized angles, and timing pitches before morning planning meetings while avoiding periods when breaking news dominates coverage.
strategic_hook: Understanding how understaffed local newsrooms operate and what information they need upfront directly informs how to design customer outreach and messaging strategy for PR and media relations campaigns targeting local markets.

heading: WHY BRANDS NEED TO FUEL A LIFE, NOT FILL A FEED (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: Gen Z increasingly rejects constant social media engagement, with 40% wishing social media had never been invented and 63% intentionally unplugging regularly—the highest rate of any generation. Pinterest argues that traditional feed-scrolling advertising fails because 44% of online sessions trap users in passive "loops" where ads are ignored, whereas intentional, action-oriented browsing generates real engagement and purchasing decisions. The company proposes a three-step marketing framework called "design the exit": open the door by showing how brands enable fuller lives rather than selling products, ignite intention by providing specific guidance and next steps to decision-making, and set them free by releasing users back to their lives rather than trapping them in experiences. Examples include Virgin Australia's "Live it" travel campaign and Starbucks Mexico's add-to-calendar Pin extension that facilitates real-world social gatherings. Pinterest reports 640 million monthly users and claims 69% say the platform leads to real-world decisions, positioning itself as the most action-oriented social platform for marketing.
strategic_hook: Understanding this generational shift away from passive scrolling and toward intentional, action-driven online behavior is essential for mapping the modern customer journey and identifying high-intent decision moments where brands can meaningfully connect with audiences.

heading: THE ART OF BRAND MERCH (8 MINUTE READ)
summary: Brand merchandise succeeds when it invites customers into a brand's world rather than simply displaying a logo, according to this analysis of merch strategy. The article examines three case studies: Glossier's iconic baby-pink packaging pouches that became collectible without a logo, Rhode's phone case designed around its lip tint that drove product sales, and Rivian's adventure-focused gear shop that lets non-customers experience the brand's lifestyle through affordable items like camp stoves and fleeces. The author argues that effective merch answers two questions: why would someone want to carry this, and what does carrying it make them part of? Practical recommendations include designing objects around actual product use, creating signature visual elements rather than relying on logos, collaborating with complementary brands, using limited releases to create scarcity, and making some merch earned through customer behaviors rather than purchased.
strategic_hook: Understanding what customers want to signal about themselves through brand merchandise can inform both product design and go-to-market strategy, particularly for building community identity and extending brand reach beyond core customers.

heading: HOW LONG SHOULD A REEL BE? UNDER 3 MINUTES ON INSTAGRAM, LONGER ON TIKTOK (12 MINUTE READ)
summary: This analysis of 10.5 million Instagram reels and 3.3 million TikToks (August 2025–September 2026) from accounts with 1,000+ followers finds that optimal video length differs sharply by platform. On Instagram, reels under 3 minutes perform within 2% of each creator's median views; reels over 3 minutes drop to 0.91x and receive no algorithmic recommendation to new audiences. On TikTok, videos of 3–10 minutes achieve 1.22x a creator's median, significantly outperforming shorter formats, likely incentivized by the Creator Rewards Program's 1-minute minimum. The research controls for creator size using per-creator comparisons rather than pooled medians, revealing that previous studies recommending 45–60 seconds conflate large accounts' posting habits with actual performance. The data shows 15 seconds is most common on both platforms, with larger creators posting longer videos overall.
strategic_hook: Brands evaluating creator partnerships should analyze a creator's own video-length performance before booking, as individual creators show vastly different returns—one dog-grooming creator gained 3.6x views on 3–10 minute videos while another farm account lost two-thirds of views at that length—requiring custom audience and content-strategy assessment rather than platform-wide guidelines.

heading: YOUR NEWSLETTER ISN'T THE UNSUBSCRIBE PROBLEM (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: A Gmail sender's "Needs work" status in Postmaster Tools for unsubscribe compliance typically isn't caused by a single newsletter platform but rather by multiple email systems sending from the same domain without synchronized suppression lists. When a subscriber unsubscribes from one system like Beehiiv, Gmail measures compliance at the domain level across all senders, so if HubSpot or another tool continues sending from that domain without knowing about the unsubscribe, Google records a compliance violation. The author explains that Google can't access individual platform suppression lists—it only observes whether mail stops after an unsubscribe—and measures this per domain, meaning one sloppy system degrades the reputation of all mail from that domain. The solution involves three steps: syncing unsubscribes across all systems, separating mail streams with distinct From addresses and List-IDs, and ensuring every system has proper one-click unsubscribe headers. Failing to fix this cascade effect means frustrated users hit spam instead of unsubscribe a second time, further damaging domain reputation and potentially affecting the newsletter's inbox placement.
strategic_hook: Understanding how multiple email systems interact across a single domain is critical for developing a customer engagement strategy that maintains sender reputation and ensures subscribers can actually opt out, directly impacting email deliverability and customer experience.

heading: A STANDING HOLDOUT IS THE ONLY AUDIT AN ALGORITHM CANNOT ARGUE WITH (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: In 2017-2021, major companies including Uber, JPMorgan Chase, Procter & Gamble, and Airbnb discovered that cutting large portions of their digital advertising spend—ranging from 66% to 99%—produced little to no measurable impact on customer acquisition or business outcomes. Uber found $100 million of its $150 million annual performance marketing budget was ineffective, Chase cut 400,000 placements down to 5,000 with no cost impact, P&G eliminated $200 million in digital spend without reducing growth rates, and Airbnb maintained 95% of pre-pandemic traffic with minimal marketing during lockdown. These discoveries occurred by accident or during crises, not through standard measurement dashboards, revealing that automated bidding systems inherently favor themselves by targeting people already close to conversion and attributing their purchases to the ads. The article argues that companies need "standing holdouts"—permanent control groups excluded from automated campaigns on a rotating schedule—as the only audit mechanism an algorithm cannot manipulate, combined with pre-registered analysis plans, protection protocols, and predetermined decision thresholds for acting on results.
strategic_hook: Understanding the true effectiveness of marketing channels through holdout testing is critical when building business cases for budget allocation, as dashboards alone cannot reveal whether spending is creating actual incremental business value or merely capturing customers who would have converted anyway.

heading: AI AGENTS BUY THROUGH YOUR OWN CHECKOUT, AND DISPUTES STILL LAND ON YOU (8 MINUTE READ)
summary: AI agents can now complete purchases on merchants' own websites using standard checkout procedures, but the legal and financial risk remains entirely with sellers. OpenAI scaled back its built-in ChatGPT checkout in March 2026, shifting buyers to complete purchases on merchant sites instead, while Google's and Microsoft's in-chat checkouts grow but remain limited to physical goods through established platforms like Shopify and Etsy. When agents buy through a seller's own checkout—as Amazon's Buy for Me, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's dots do—they use the merchant's payment processor and existing wallet systems like Stripe's Link or Google Pay. Visa's rules designate the cardholder as responsible for an agent's actions with no liability shift to the agent provider, and Stripe's terms explicitly make sellers handle disputes, refunds, and fraud. Currently, AI assistants drive negligible traffic: Frankfurt School research found chatbot referrals under 0.2% of visits, and Shopify merchants received just 0.12% of revenue from AI agents. The article recommends sellers optimize their own checkouts for agent completion, maintain clear product pricing and schema markup, allow guest purchases, and only join in-chat programs if they match the seller's product type.
strategic_hook: Understanding how AI agents navigate customer journeys differently than human buyers—requiring guest checkouts, saved payment methods, and bot-verified pathways—is essential for mapping the emerging agent-driven customer journey and identifying necessary changes to conversion funnels and payment infrastructure.

heading: YOUR TEAM SAYS AI SAVES THEM TIME. HERE'S HOW TO FIND OUT IF IT DOES (15 MINUTE READ)
summary: Companies frequently report that AI saves them time, but research shows these self-assessments are unreliable; in a 2025 METR trial, software developers believed AI had accelerated their work by 20%, yet actual measurement showed tasks took 19% longer. The article identifies six common ways organizations evaluate AI success—what staff say, what executives observe, human oversight, published failure rates, vendor case studies, and audits—and demonstrates how each can systematically mislead. AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have recognized that the bottleneck isn't AI capability but "knowing whether it works," with Anthropic advertising a Technical Deployment Lead role focused on "value measurement and ROI" at a base salary of up to $380,000. The author proposes a six-step testing framework adapted from hospitals, airports, and banks: pick one process and one measurable outcome, measure current performance, decide which steps AI should handle, present AI recommendations at the moment of decision, run the AI version alongside the old process while testing human reviewers' ability to catch planted errors, and continue monitoring after deployment. Real measured gains have been modest—customer support improved 15%, AI note-takers saved 41 seconds per note, and four of seven retail AI uses raised sales by up to 16.3%—while government audits of the IRS and Australian Taxation Office found no regular monitoring after deployment began.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: AMAZON LAUNCHES NEW BEE ‘PERSONAL AI' DEVICES THAT LISTEN TO CONVERSATIONS (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Amazon released two new Bee always-listening AI devices on October 15, 2026: the Bee Frontier, a wearable bracelet priced at $75 with upgraded noise filtering and seven-day battery life, and the Bee Eclipse, a $100 credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to smartphones. These devices mark the first update to Amazon's Bee lineup since acquiring the San Francisco startup in July 2025, as the company competes with other AI wearables like Meta's smart glasses and Plaud's card-shaped note-taking device during the holiday shopping season. The Bee devices continuously record conversations and offer features like summaries, memory reviews, and trend tracking, with an optional $12/month Bee Pro subscription providing unlimited summaries and integrations with Amazon services. Amazon claims users' data is encrypted and inaccessible even to Amazon itself, with an LED indicator showing when recording is active.
strategic_hook: none

heading: TELLING AI TO ACT AS YOUR CUSTOMERS MAKES ITS ANSWER WORSE (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: The author built PlebTest, an AI tool that simulates customer personas to give founders feedback on product ideas without conducting real customer interviews, aiming for 1,000 paying users by end of 2026. However, two pre-registered studies published in 2026 showed AI persona panels systematically overestimate customer interest: in one supermarket study, personas predicted 52% purchase rate versus 33% actual, and 32% coupon redemption versus 14% real; in a headline-ranking study, personas scored 0.084 on ranking accuracy versus 0.361 for plain model queries. The author never validated PlebTest against real customers and ultimately killed the product in August, discovering that the persona layer—built as the core feature—made predictions worse, not better. Research shows that calibrating fake customers requires 50–300 real customer responses, which defeats the purpose of avoiding real conversations entirely. The author now advocates using AI personas only for brainstorming objections, practicing conversations, and comparing versions with plain queries—never for purchase verdicts.
strategic_hook: When building customer research tools or services, founders must validate their research methodology itself against actual customer behavior before scaling; assuming a method works without comparing predictions to real purchase or engagement data will produce systematically biased outputs that misguide downstream business decisions.

heading: GOOGLE'S WHEN TO BUY GUIDE (8 MINUTE READ)
summary: Google released a 2026 "When to Buy Guide" analyzing historical promotional patterns and search trends across U.S. merchants to help consumers time their holiday purchases optimally. The guide maps peak discount periods across major product categories, revealing that Black Friday weekend offers the best deals and selection for most items like electronics, apparel, and toys, while late December provides steepest markdowns on clearance inventory for categories like kitchen items, gaming consoles, and fitness equipment. For specific categories, Google recommends split strategies—for example, buying women's apparel with must-have sizes during Black Friday but waiting until late December for flexible wardrobe refreshes. The analysis also reveals behavioral patterns showing that men's gifts receive last-minute shopping more than women's gifts, that New Yorkers consistently procrastinate on holiday purchases, and that December 22-24 trigger peak searches for next-day shipping, DIY gifts, local pickup options, and digital gift cards as delivery deadlines pass. Google calculated these insights using impression-weighted methodology across its merchant data to track both discount coverage and discount depth by category throughout the season.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: GATED CONTENT IS THE #1 ENEMY OF AI SEARCH (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: AI search systems like ChatGPT and Claude cannot access gated content behind forms or paywalls, making such assets invisible to LLM crawlers and excluding them from both training datasets and real-time retrieval systems. While B2B companies traditionally gated high-value assets like whitepapers, webinars, and research reports to generate marketing-qualified leads, this approach now conflicts with how modern buyers research vendors—they rely on AI systems to discover recommendations before ever contacting sales. The problem is compounded because gated content only exposes AI crawlers to splash pages with minimal value, allowing competitors with ungated content to receive citations and brand authority instead. MQLs generated from gated content historically had poor conversion rates anyway, yet the practice persists. The article recommends ungating educational content that helps buyers understand categories, evaluate products, or compare vendors, while reserving hard gates only for genuinely exclusive assets like licensed analyst reports, personalized ROI audits, or proprietary calculators. Strategies include publishing research summaries and key findings openly while gating full PDFs, using noindex tags to prevent PDF cannibalization, and prioritizing HTML pillar pages for SEO and AI indexing.
strategic_hook: Understanding how AI search systems influence the modern B2B buyer journey is essential to mapping customer research behavior and informing content strategy decisions about which assets drive actual consideration versus lead capture.

heading: YOUR NEXT MARKETING HIRE SHOULD PROBABLY SURPRISE YOU (6 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article argues that software companies should fundamentally rethink their marketing hiring strategy by recruiting talent from entertainment and creator backgrounds rather than traditional marketing. As AI commoditizes content production and consideration-stage marketing, the author contends that the competitive advantage has shifted to the awareness stage, where companies need people who can make products culturally interesting and shareable. The author identifies three critical new roles: Viral Producers who run creative experiments (exemplified by Ramp's team that created the Kevin from The Office glass box campaign), Internet Comedians who create meme-worthy brand content (citing Meta's Muse mascot strategy), and Creator Deal Makers who structure mutually beneficial partnerships with influencers (like HubSpot's approach of offering audience cross-promotion and locked CPM rates). The core insight is that traditional marketing optimization has made B2B marketing sound corporate and soulless, while companies that hire comedy writers, producers, and entertainment strategists are winning cultural relevance and word-of-mouth growth in an AI-saturated content landscape.
strategic_hook: When identifying which customer segments have shifted their research behavior to AI assistants and social platforms, a Customer Strategy exercise should assess whether your current marketing talent can authentically reach these audiences through entertainment and shareability—informing whether to restructure your marketing team composition before your competitors do.

heading: SAVE YOUR SPOT →
summary: This is an event announcement for a webinar featuring Evan Hamilton, HubSpot's Director of Community (formerly at Reddit), discussing effective B2B strategies for Reddit. Hamilton will share lessons from five years inside Reddit managing moderators alongside his experience building HubSpot's Reddit presence, covering what brands commonly get wrong about subreddit culture, tactics that failed for HubSpot, the role of brand versus personal accounts, and how Reddit fits into AI search opportunities. The event emphasizes that successful Reddit engagement requires earning trust with moderators and treating communities as experiments rather than following shortcuts that lead to bans. The webinar is hosted by Standing on Giants, a 15-year-old community management agency that works with brands like Airbnb and Lenovo on platforms including Reddit and Discord.

heading: HOW TO AUTOMATE CONTENT CREATION: A FOLLOW-ALONG GUIDE (16 MINUTE READ)
summary: Ahrefs created an automated system called the Data Refresh Hub that pulls fresh data monthly for twelve datasets, filters out irrelevant results, rebuilds tables and charts, updates WordPress drafts, and alerts the author for review before publication—handling repetitive content maintenance tasks while preserving human judgment. The author emphasizes that automation should target boring, repetitive work (like updating data-driven articles monthly instead of quarterly) rather than replacing creative decisions, and shares a seven-step methodology: choose one repeatable task, document your exact process including shortcuts and unwritten rules, connect the system to reliable data sources rather than relying on LLM hallucinations, provide examples of good and bad outputs with explicit reasoning, test thoroughly on a single piece before scaling, run a full trial and compare against human-made versions, and gradually expand to other articles. Critical to the approach is maintaining human review at every stage, keeping rejected outputs visible to catch mistakes, generating intermediate outputs at each workflow stage for debugging, scheduling after data sources refresh, setting up failure alerts, and anticipating ongoing maintenance because model updates, API changes, and rule drift will eventually break any automation. The core philosophy is using AI to eliminate tedious parts of content creation so teams can focus on ideas, opinions, and expertise that models cannot replicate.
strategic_hook: Understanding the business case for content automation requires mapping the customer journey of content creators (identifying time-drains versus value-add activities) and competitor analysis of publishing cadence—this framework helps prioritize which customer needs automation can serve without compromising quality or brand voice.

heading: HOW THE AI BOOM MIGHT REALLY END: 5 SCENARIOS (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article outlines five scenarios where the AI investment boom could unwind, organized into two categories. Group 1 covers direct AI failures: models hitting scaling walls with diminishing returns, catastrophic alignment failures triggering political backlash and GPU demand collapse, or datacentre bans (though the author sees these as unlikely due to geopolitical competition). Group 2, deemed more probable, covers scenarios where AI succeeds but value doesn't flow to capital investors: open-source models becoming competitive enough to collapse frontier lab margins (with Anthropic's Haiku 5.5 now 90% cheaper and competing with open weights), or massive efficiency breakthroughs in hardware or software that outpace token demand growth. The author argues the real risk is not that AI stops working, but that tokens flow to more players at lower margins, and that leverage in the sector amplifies downside risk—citing CoreWeave's distressed credit default swaps as evidence that financing fragility, not demand destruction, could trigger unraveling.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: WHAT ON EARTH IS GOING ON WITH AI PRICING AND PACKAGING? (8 MINUTE READ)
summary: AI companies are struggling with fundamentally broken pricing and packaging strategies that obscure rather than clarify value. Products like Grok multiply unknown usage numbers by multipliers, Muse offers 500 million tokens weekly without explaining what they buy, and even major players like OpenAI and Anthropic use vague descriptors like "More" and "Maximum" without concrete baselines. The root cause is that AI's general-purpose nature makes traditional consumption metrics (seats, storage, API calls) obsolete, while unpredictable inference costs and variable customer workloads make outcome-based pricing risky for vendors. Though early adopters tolerate this opacity because AI products deliver genuine value, mass-market adoption requires transparent, predictable pricing aligned with customer outcomes rather than mysterious credits and impossible-to-forecast token budgets. Whoever solves AI pricing first—making costs understandable and tied to deliverable value—will gain significant competitive advantage.
strategic_hook: Understanding how customers actually evaluate and justify AI tool purchases through clear, predictable pricing communication is essential for market segmentation strategy and identifying which customer personas will drive mainstream adoption versus remaining locked in early-adopter markets.

heading: CHATGPT ADVERTISERS REPORT MIXED RESULTS AS TARGETING PROBLEMS PERSIST (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: OpenAI's ChatGPT advertising pilot is generating revenue quickly, hitting a $1 billion annualized run rate in under 200 days, but early results are highly inconsistent. Advertisers report mixed outcomes: while some achieve cost-per-acquisition figures 15.3% lower than paid search benchmarks, others spend hundreds of dollars with zero conversions. The core problem is targeting—approximately 14% of ads have limited or no connection to user queries, and the platform struggles to distinguish between curious researchers and actual buyers, resulting in click-through rates between 0.5% and 2% with cost-per-click ranging from under $3 to over $10. Most advertisers are treating ChatGPT ads as small-scale experiments rather than core channels pending data improvement. OpenAI has rolled out better measurement tools and new creative formats in response to feedback, and results from partnership deals look more promising than self-serve performance.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: BOTS USED TO BE A THREAT. NOW THEY'RE YOUR CUSTOMERS (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: Bots now constitute 53% of web traffic and are evolving from simple scrapers into AI agents that actively execute workflows on behalf of consumers, fundamentally changing how customers discover and purchase products. Traditional bot-blocking defenses that brands built over thirty years now inadvertently exclude legitimate AI agents like ChatGPT and Claude, causing these agents to route around poorly-structured websites to easier-to-access marketplaces and competitors. Brands must shift from a defensive posture to treating bots as a first-class audience by auditing their bot policies, structuring data accessibly (pricing, inventory, reviews), optimizing for agent workflows (product discovery, comparisons, checkout), and revamping analytics to track impressions across AI search surfaces rather than just on-site visits. The risk of inaction is silent: customers ask their AI assistants for recommendations, the agent finds your product but abandons your site due to friction, and you never see the lost consideration in analytics. This requires architectural changes to website design and data structure that extend well beyond traditional SEO or marketing tweaks.
strategic_hook: Brands need to map the emerging agent-assisted customer journey to identify critical decision points (product discovery, comparison, purchase) where friction causes agents to route toward competitors, then prioritize site structure and data accessibility to support these new buying paths.
